key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the circumstantial evidence and the last seen theory, but found the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses to be untrustworthy due to serious contradictions.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses (PWs 1 to 3) as completely untrustworthy due to serious contradictions in their evidence, which the Sessions Court and High Court trivialized.

legal_representation.accused: S. Nagamuthu, Sr. Adv., Ms. Shivani Misra, Harsh Parashar, Chanakya Sharma, Ms. Chetna Bhargava, D. S. Vairawan, R. Sudhakaran, G. R. Vikash, Subrahmanya Bhanu, Advs.
legal_representation.state: Ardhendumauli Kumar Prasad, AAG, Parmanand Pandey, Ms. Shreya Srivastava, Ashish Madaan, Ms. Ananya Sahu, Aman Singh Bhadauria, Utkarsh Pandey, Advs.

investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
procedural_irregularity: Delay of five days in transmitting the FIR to the jurisdictional court was fatal; failure of the prosecution to subject the accused to medical examination when ocular evidence is untrustworthy was certainly fatal

appeal_history.supreme_court: Allowed the appeals, set aside the conviction and sentence

prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant was guilty of raping and murdering a six-year-old girl based on circumstantial evidence, including the last seen theory and the testimonies of PWs 1 to 3. They claimed the evidence was trustworthy and that the chain of circumstances was unbroken.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the testimonies of PWs 1 to 3 were untrustworthy due to serious contradictions, the delay in forwarding the FIR to the court, and the failure of the prosecution to conduct a medical examination of the accused, which created a gaping hole in the prosecution's case.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that for a conviction based on circumstantial evidence, the chain of circumstances must be complete, unbroken, and exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved.
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116; Meharaj Singh (L/Nk.) v. State of U.P (1994) 5 SCC 188; Bhajan Singh alias Harbhajan Singh and Others v. State of Haryana (2011) 7 SCC 421; Brahm Swaroop and Another v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2011) 6 SCC 288; Balram Singh and Another v. State of Punjab (2003) 11 SCC 286; State of Rajasthan v. Daud Khan (2016) 2 SCC 607; Jafarudheen and Ors. v. State of Kerala 2022 SCC Online SC 495; Krishan Kumar Malik v. State of Haryana (2011) 7 SCC 130; Rajendra Pralhadrao Wasnik v. State of Maharashtra (2019) 12 SCC 460
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed by the lower courts as a 'rarest of rare' case where a six-year-old girl was raped and murdered. However, the Supreme Court found the conviction and sentence to be based on untrustworthy evidence and overturned the verdict.
other_sentence_order: The appellant was to be released forthwith if not wanted in connection with any other case.
